title: Hubble Spots a Glittering City of Ancient Stars
summary:
Look closely at this glittering crowd of stars. Some of them are almost as old as the universe itself — and they may hold clues to how our Milky Way formed.

The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars shining like cosmic jewels in blue, gold and orange. The image, released by the European Space Agency on November 5, shows Messier 30, known as M30, a densely packed collection of stars about 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster: a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars, all held together by gravity. Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings. Some are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old.

Globular clusters are like cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. That is what makes a pretty picture into a scientific treasure.

M30 also has a strange story of its own. Astronomers have discovered that it travels through the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. Several other globular clusters do the same. That unusual motion raises an intriguing possibility: M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. Instead, it could have been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago, a visitor from somewhere else that never left.

So the next time you look up at the night sky, remember: some of those tiny points of light have been shining since almost the beginning of time.
why_it_matters: Studying ancient star clusters helps scientists learn how our own galaxy formed, and it reminds us that the night sky holds clues to the very beginning of the universe.

background_read: The Hubble Space Telescope is a large telescope in space that takes pictures of stars, galaxies, and other faraway objects.
A globular cluster is a tightly packed, ball-shaped group of very many stars that are all held together by gravity.
Because the stars in these clusters are so old, studying them can tell scientists about the early days of a galaxy like the Milky Way.
Some clusters move in unusual ways, which can hint that they did not start out in the galaxy they now travel through.
